title: Keeping It Simple With Oral Exams
author: Robert Talbert
summary: A university mathematics instructor describes and evaluates his first small-scale oral exam system, piloted in a 13-student sophomore course on communicating in mathematics. Each student took one 15 to 20 minute exam at the whiteboard on a portfolio problem they had already completed and received feedback on, graded Successful or Not Yet with up to three attempts. His motive was to improve the incentives for genuine human work and reduce the temptation to offload thinking to an LLM, not to "AI-proof" the course. Results were good: nearly everyone passed on the first try, extension questions showed real understanding, and students enjoyed the format. The costs were also clear, including about four extra hours of meetings, a narrow pool of eligible problems, and doubt about whether students learned anything new rather than simply memorizing. He plans to keep the exams while changing the timing and the rules to ease the time burden.
points: Oral exams give a proctored check on deep individual understanding of work students completed unproctored, similar in purpose to written mastery exams.
Basing the exam on a previously completed, feedback-reviewed problem kept the format low-stakes, with a Successful or Not Yet mark and up to three attempts.
A fresh extension question and a request to solve a problem a different way helped convince him that students understood rather than memorized.
The main cost is instructor time, about four extra hours for just 13 students, plus the constraint of only asking about problems students had finished.
He leans toward keeping oral exams but delaying them, and is weighing giving a list of unfinished problems or choosing from a small group at the meeting.
quotes: The common idea of both mastery exams and oral exams is to check that students have a deep individual understanding of some fundamental ideas.
not to “AI-proof” the course, which I think is a fool’s errand, but to improve the incentives to do genuine human-created work and reduce the temptations to offload thinking to an AI.
Overall, the goal is to explain your logic, and to show that you have a thorough individual understanding of it.
Almost every student passed the oral exam on their first attempt, with a few needing one reassessment. Nobody ran up against the three-attempt limit.
For me, one of the joys of the oral exams was how they gave students a chance to shine in a different way, one that I don’t normally get to see.
Did students really learn anything new through this process? That’s unclear. Perhaps all I did was make them jump through another hoop on something they already understood perfectly well.
The single biggest issue I encountered with the oral exams was the amount of time it took for me to meet with every student for 15-20 minutes.
I do enjoy getting to talk directly with students, to quiz them one on one, and to cheer them on.
